claims.text: The target materials are rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys in a disordered solid-solution state.
The initial alloys may contain nanoscale precipitates.
Varying annealing temperature and time can adjust lattice strain.
Varying annealing temperature and time can adjust the size and volume fraction of nanoscale precipitates.
Optimized annealing reduces local variations in lattice strain.
Optimized annealing standardizes nanoscale precipitate features and produces a homogeneous precipitate distribution.
Reduced local strain variation narrows the distribution of magnetic exchange energies.
Standardized nanoscale precipitate features narrow the distribution of magnetic exchange energies.
A narrower distribution of magnetic exchange energies amplifies the magnetocaloric effect at low applied fields.
Optimized annealing improves the low-field magnetocaloric response without compromising heat-exchange efficiency.
Optimized annealing improves the low-field magnetocaloric response without compromising mechanical stability.
Optimally annealed samples will exhibit a stronger low-field magnetocaloric response than non-optimally treated samples.
Optimally annealed samples will exhibit lower magnetic hysteresis than non-optimally treated samples.
Optimally annealed samples will sustain rapid heat exchange relative to non-optimally treated samples.
Optimally annealed samples will retain mechanical integrity relative to non-optimally treated samples.
Samples produced without controlled annealing have more heterogeneous lattice strain.
Samples produced without controlled annealing have less consistent nanoscale precipitate formation.
Heterogeneous lattice strain and inconsistent precipitate formation produce a wider distribution of magnetic exchange energies.
The proposed relationship is expected to hold for disordered rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys under low-field operation and rapid thermal and mechanical cycling.
